problemTitle: D1 says a table doesn't exist even though a migration created it
problemSummary: A query against D1 fails with "no such table" even though a migration that creates the table has been written and appears to have run, because it was applied to the wrong target (local vs remote) or against the wrong database.
title: Fixing D1 "no such table" after a migration that seemed to run
summary: Covers the two most common causes: applying a migration to the wrong local/remote target, and a Worker binding pointing at a different database_id than the one that was migrated. Does not cover a migration file that itself has a SQL error (that fails loudly at apply time, not later as "no such table"), or drift specifically caused by an ORM's own migration tracking — see the Drizzle-specific playbook for that. Also covers a preview_database_id on the binding sending wrangler dev to a different database from the one the migration was applied to.
symptoms: A query fails with D1_ERROR: no such table: <table>, or SQLITE_ERROR: no such table
You're confident the migration file that creates the table exists and looks correct
The table shows up when queried against one environment (e.g. local) but not another (e.g. remote), or vice versa

nodes.title: D1 query fails with "no such table"
nodes.body: A SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE against a table fails as if it were never created, despite a migration existing for it.

nodes.title: Check which database the migration actually ran against
nodes.body: D1 local and remote are separate SQLite databases. `wrangler d1 migrations apply` needs an explicit `--local` or `--remote` flag, and running it once with one flag does not apply it to the other.
nodes.expectedOutput: The migration you expect is listed under migrations still to be applied, rather than under already-applied ones.

nodes.title: Apply the migration to the target that's missing it
nodes.body: Run migrations apply against whichever target the failing query is actually hitting — typically `--remote` for a deployed Worker, `--local` for `wrangler dev`.
nodes.safetyEffect: Applies any pending .sql migration files to the remote D1 database, creating or altering tables as those files specify. It does not delete existing data unless a migration file itself contains a DROP or DELETE statement.

nodes.title: Check whether the binding points at a different database
nodes.body: Confirm the `database_id` your deployed Worker is actually bound to matches the one you migrated — a stale `preview_database_id`, or a staging/production database_id mix-up in wrangler.jsonc, will produce exactly this symptom even after a correct migration run.
nodes.expectedOutput: The database_id shown does not match the database_id in the d1_databases block your Worker is deployed with.

nodes.title: Point the binding at the correct database and redeploy
nodes.body: Correct the `database_id` (and `preview_database_id` if relevant) in your Wrangler configuration to match the database that actually has the migration applied, then redeploy.
nodes.safetyEffect: Redeploys the Worker so it binds to the D1 database that has the migration applied. No data in either database is modified by this step.

nodes.title: Not a target/binding mismatch — escalate
nodes.body: If the migration is applied to the right database and the binding is correct, check whether `migrations_table` was customised away from the default and the table really was created but under a name or in a way you're not querying — or check the migration file itself for a typo in the table name.

nodes.title: Confirm the table exists where you're querying it
nodes.body: List the tables directly against the same target (local/remote) your Worker queries at runtime.
nodes.command: npx wrangler d1 execute <DATABASE_NAME> --remote --command "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';"
nodes.expectedOutput: The table you expected appears in the result set.

nodes.title: Resolved
nodes.body: The correct database has the migration applied and the Worker is bound to that database; the query now succeeds.

nodes.title: Check whether the binding has a preview_database_id
nodes.body: A D1 binding may carry both `database_id` and `preview_database_id`. `wrangler dev` connects to the **preview** one when it is set, and `wrangler d1 migrations apply` targets the database you name on the command line — so the two can be different databases while both fields look correct.
nodes.expectedOutput: A preview_database_id is present in wrangler.jsonc and names a different database from database_id.

nodes.title: Apply the migration to the preview database, or remove the preview binding
nodes.body: Either apply the migration to the preview database as well, or drop `preview_database_id` so local development uses the same database as deployment. Applying to both is usually right while the schema is still moving; removing it is right once it has settled.
nodes.safetyEffect: Applies pending migration files to the preview D1 database, creating or altering tables as those files specify.

changeSummary: Adds a third cause. The original revision handled a migration applied to the wrong local/remote target and a binding pointing at the wrong database_id, then escalated. It had no branch for a preview_database_id set on the binding, which is what wrangler dev actually connects to — so a reader whose migration and database_id were both correct reached “escalate” with the real cause unexamined. New test node and fix inserted on the path that previously dead-ended.
